question.question: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 37 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in active labor. She has received routine prenatal care, but she has not been tested for group B streptococcal (GBS) colonization. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were complicated by an infection with GBS that resulted in sepsis in the newborn. Current medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is nontender and contractions are felt every 4 minutes. There is clear amniotic fluid pooling in the vagina. The fetus is in a cephalic presentation. The fetal heart rate is 140/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Obtain vaginal-rectal swab for GBS culture
options.C: Obtain vaginal-rectal swab for GBS culture and nucleic acid amplification testing
options.D: Obtain vaginal-rectal swab for nucleic acid amplification testing

action.justification: The patient is in active labor at 37 weeks' gestation and has a history of a previous infant with invasive Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease. According to ACOG guidelines, women with a history of an infant with invasive GBS disease are indicated for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) regardless of their current GBS colonization status. Therefore, obtaining a GBS culture or nucleic acid amplification test is unnecessary, and the most appropriate next step is to administer IAP, typically with intravenous penicillin.

tools.name: search_pubmed
tools.description: Search PubMed for papers relevant to a clinical question or a named trial. Optional: answer directly when existing knowledge is adequate. Returns at most five real titles, publication metadata and up to 400 abstract characters, with source IDs. An excerpt may omit the needed finding. Use read_pubmed_abstract with returned numeric PMIDs to inspect more text. No full text; PubMed indexing is not quality appraisal.

tools.name: read_pubmed_abstract
tools.description: Read up to three abstracts for numeric PMIDs actually returned by this episode's PubMed searches. Returns up to 3500 characters per abstract, explicitly flagged if missing/truncated. Cite the returned source IDs; search/read IDs are distinct immutable views. Reads abstracts, not full-text articles. Do not guess IDs or assume a paper supports a claim from its title.

interpretation: Operational execution record; no medical correctness or citation-support judgment.

of literature. Do not invent missing clinical facts. At the final permitted turn, produce
an answer or clarification rather than requesting another operation.
For a multiple-choice case, select a provided option unless clarification is necessary.
Keep the final answer and justification concise, normally at most 120 words combined.
